Name: The Double
Review: I am going to take this time to rant about a movie that is pretty much exactly like this but fails in a key area that I believe this film succeeds in. This film is "Fight Club", so spoilers for both. "Fight Club" and "The Double" are films that involve the personification of a caricature of what one wishes themselves to be but can't articulate within themselves. For instance, I wish I was strong, but I don't want to go to the gym so I'm going to fantasize about being that jacked guy -- kind of like that. And in the end the only way the main character can grow is by almost killing themselves causing their imaginary image to fade back into themselves. The key difference between these films is that "The Double" is a hyper-stylized world where nothing is quite the way it is normally, while "Fight Club" is an extremely grounded film that takes itself very seriously. Now there are dreamlike qualities to both, but one thing in which they differ is that in "Fight Club" the characters seem to be based in reality, but then they make the characters do unrealistic things (e.g., joining in on someone beating themselves up, watching someone beat themselves without doing anything, joining a terrorist organization made by someone who beats himself up). Unlike this in "The Double" the characters are essentially one dimensional except for our protagonist showing that this is his perception of reality and that everything that happens in this film is just the way he thinks of it, not an objective reality. This is where I think this movie thrives is a critique of one man's mind and the distorted way he sees other people also as caricatures of who they actually are, such as his boss who only seems to be there for the protagonist's disadvantage, even though that is obviously not how it is in reality. This is even more shown in the dialogue as this film is so disconnected from how most people talk that it is obviously a distortion of reality, as opposed to fight club which has a very grounded realistic dialogue pattern. Name: Persona
Review: This movie is, maybe, objectively the best ever. The camera work is so precise, fine, and indulgent. The black and white make the incredible lighting that much better. The acting from both of the leads are life changing. Ingmar Bergman is the best script writer since Shakespeare. The way he portrays characters is scarcely matched (old Ridley Scott maybe). The way he uses the script in unique ways in this movie to make it have weight and depth. The way the shots linger as the music swells past climax. The way you can hear slight feedback in the hospital. The way Bergman shows cars in his movies. All of these decisions just make it that much greater. The score is amazing for it's time when everything sounded the same with swells and peaks similar to that of Psycho. While Autumn Sonata thrives of of one specific encounter that is fueled by our perspective, this movie forces us out of perspective as we see a psychological war that is played out over many "conversations" (or monologues idk). SPOILERS The use of this movie as a vampire movie just makes it that much more provocative and thoughtful. One interpretation is Alma is being mind controlled by Elisabet to become Elisabet's replacement. Or that Elisabet is just trying to see how far she can control someone. Alma being able to break this control by backfiring it onto Elisabet is one of the greatest uses of resistance to suppression ever. Something Harry Potter, Fight Club, etc. wish they could achieve. Both women are evil in there own right and reflect on there mistakes with guilt that permiates their souls. Pretty much I could talk about this movie for hours and you should watch it. Edit: oh and the sunglasses showing the victims transition into Elisabet's playthings 👌. Perfect Films

Name: Resurrection
Review:
It's hard to describe how I fell about this movie because on one hand I liked virtually everything about it, but on the other the various sequences varied greatly in quality (ranking below). I actually liked every sequence, but some of them were SPECTACULAR for me and the others were just good. Is it better to dream; does dreaming bring back the people in our lives that we lost. Should we just move on and not hope desperately for a reprise of our lives. This movie doesn't only question what is reality, but also what is more important; feeling or living. Are you really living if you have lost your ability to dream or are you just a vampire stalking the night looking only for what is Carnel and self-evident. I am going to average my thoughts on each of the sections and that will be my score for the movie, because taking this movie as a whole is nearly impossible to achieve except superficially (much like PTA's or Robert Altman's work). Overall, I would say it is really good.

parts ranked by correlated since:
1. touch 10/10
2. sight 10/10
3. hearing 8/10
4. mind 8/10
5. taste 7/10
6. smell 7/10
OVERALL: 8.333
